title: Review: Chemistry — Chemical reactions
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for KS3 Science (chemistry) (status of the source: authored-reviewed-reverified-2026-10-08). Terms and clues: C4.4#xt2 term and clue written for the game; C4.2#xt1 term and clue written for the game; C4.8#xt3 term and clue written for the game; C4#c19 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Antacid
items.clue: A medicine containing a substance that neutralises excess acid in the stomach

items.label: Subscript number
items.clue: The small, low digit in a formula showing how many atoms of one type there are

items.label: Catalytic converter
items.clue: Part of a car exhaust where a precious metal speeds up changes to harmful gases

items.label: Indicator
items.clue: A substance that changes colour depending on how acidic or alkaline a solution is.

questions.stem: A student adds an alkali to an acid. A reaction happens, but there is no fizzing. Why?

options.text: The gas made has dissolved in the water
The hydrogen made is too light to see
The reaction is too slow to make bubbles
The products are a salt and water, not a gas

questions.explanation: An acid and an alkali make a salt plus water. No gas is made, so there are no bubbles.

questions.stem: A factory can speed up a reaction by heating it or by using a catalyst. Why might a catalyst be the better choice?

options.text: It speeds up the reaction without extra heating
It makes more product from the same reactants
It is a cheap reactant that gets used up
It heats the mixture using its own energy

questions.explanation: A catalyst speeds up a reaction at a lower temperature, so less energy is needed for heating.

questions.stem: Which acid and alkali react to make the salt potassium nitrate, plus water?

options.text: Sulfuric acid and potassium hydroxide
Nitric acid and sodium hydroxide
Nitric acid and potassium hydroxide
Nitric acid and potassium chloride

questions.explanation: Nitric acid gives nitrates, and the potassium comes from the alkali, potassium hydroxide.

questions.stem: Manganese(IV) oxide speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. Afterwards, any solid left is filtered off and dried, with none spilled. How does its mass compare with the start?

options.text: It is the same as at the start
It is less, as some was used up
It is zero, as it became the oxygen
It is more, as it took in oxygen

questions.explanation: Yes. Manganese(IV) oxide is a catalyst: it speeds up the reaction but is not used up, so the same mass is recovered.

questions.stem: Alkali is added to an acid until the pH is exactly 7. The water is then evaporated. What is left?

options.text: Nothing, as they cancel out
A salt formed by the reaction
The acid and alkali, unchanged
The alkali, as the acid broke down

questions.explanation: Yes. acid + alkali → salt + water. When the water is evaporated, the solid salt is left behind.

questions.stem: Which statement about a catalyst is correct?

options.text: It speeds up a reaction but is used up
It makes a reaction give more product
It speeds up a reaction and is not used up
It changes which products are made

questions.explanation: Yes. A catalyst makes a reaction go faster and is left over unchanged at the end, so it can be used again.

questions.stem: A student makes a salt by adding an alkali to an acid. Why is an indicator used?

options.text: To make the acid and alkali react faster
To give the salt crystals their colour
To show when the acid is just neutralised
To start the acid reacting with the alkali

questions.explanation: The indicator changes colour when just enough alkali has been added to neutralise the acid.

questions.stem: A car's catalytic converter contains the metal platinum, a catalyst. What does the platinum do?

options.text: Filters harmful gases out of the exhaust
Burns away as it reacts with harmful gases
Speeds up reactions that change harmful gases
Gives the engine extra energy from the fuel

questions.explanation: The catalyst speeds up reactions that turn harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones.

questions.stem: Hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide solution, an alkali. What are the products?

options.text: Sodium chloride and water
Sodium chloride and hydrogen
Only the acid, now diluted
Nothing, as they cancel out

questions.explanation: Yes. acid + alkali → salt + water. Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, so the salt is sodium chloride.

questions.stem: Manganese oxide speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. Why is it left out of the reactants in the equation?

options.text: Only a tiny amount of it is needed
It is not used up in the reaction
It is a solid, and reactants are liquids
It reacts too quickly to be recorded

questions.explanation: A catalyst is not used up or changed into a product, so it is not a reactant.

questions.stem: Sodium sulfate is made when an acid reacts with an alkali. Where does the 'sulfate' part of the salt come from?

options.text: From the acid, sulfuric acid
From the alkali, sodium hydroxide
From the water that is made
From sulfur in the air around

questions.explanation: The second part of a salt's name comes from the acid: sulfuric acid makes sulfates.

questions.stem: A reaction takes 60 s. With 1 g of powder X added it takes 10 s, and 1 g of X is recovered afterwards. What is X?

options.text: A reactant, as it was added at the start
A product, as it was there at the end
A fuel, as it gave the reaction energy
A catalyst, as it sped things up unchanged

questions.explanation: X made the reaction faster and its mass did not change, so it is a catalyst.
